c1-diskursmarker.title: Sophisticated Discourse Markers
c1-diskursmarker.pattern: nichtsdestotrotz, gleichwohl, insofern, immerhin, zumal, ohnehin, letztlich
c1-diskursmarker.explanation: C1 writing and speech relies on a richer set of discourse markers than B2: "nichtsdestotrotz"/"gleichwohl" (nevertheless, more formal than "trotzdem"), "insofern" (in that respect / to that extent), "immerhin" (at least / after all, softening a concession), "zumal" (especially since, adding a reinforcing reason), "ohnehin" (anyway, regardless), "letztlich" (ultimately). These words let a speaker signal precise logical relationships between ideas.
c1-diskursmarker.fact: "Zumal" is distinctive: it adds a reason that strengthens a point already made, always trailing after it: "Wir sollten jetzt gehen, zumal es schon spät ist" (We should go now, especially since it's already late) — it never opens a sentence, unlike "weil", which marks it as fundamentally an afterthought-reinforcement word, not a plain causal conjunction.

dialogue.native: Das Projekt war schwierig, aber letztlich hat es sich gelohnt.

c1-idiome.title: Idiomatic Expressions
c1-idiome.pattern: fixed figurative phrases: den Nagel auf den Kopf treffen, ins Wasser fallen, Schwein haben ...
c1-idiome.explanation: Idioms are fixed expressions whose meaning can't be derived from their individual words, and mastering them is a hallmark of near-native fluency: "den Nagel auf den Kopf treffen" (to hit the nail on the head — to say exactly the right thing), "ins Wasser fallen" (to fall through / be cancelled, literally "to fall into the water"), "Schwein haben" (to be lucky, literally "to have pig"), "die Daumen drücken" (to keep one's fingers crossed, literally "press the thumbs"), "um den heißen Brei herumreden" (to beat around the bush, literally "talk around the hot porridge").
c1-idiome.fact: Idioms resist word-by-word translation by definition — the only reliable way to acquire them is exposure and repetition in context, never analysis of the individual words. Trying to logic out an idiom's meaning from its parts is usually a trap, not a shortcut.

dialogue.native: Unser Ausflug ist wegen des Wetters ins Wasser gefallen.

dialogue.native: Schade! Aber du hast den Nagel auf den Kopf getroffen: nächstes Mal planen wir einen Plan B.

c1-regionalismen.title: Regional Vocabulary: Recognizing Austrian and Swiss Standard German
c1-regionalismen.pattern: Jänner (AT) = Januar; Sackerl (AT) = Tüte; Rahm (AT/CH) = Sahne; Velo (CH) = Fahrrad; Grüezi (CH) = Hallo
c1-regionalismen.explanation: Standard German (Hochdeutsch) itself varies by country: Austria and Switzerland have their own standardized vocabulary for everyday words, which a fluent speaker should be able to recognize even without using them actively. Examples: "Jänner" (Austrian for "Januar"), "Sackerl" (Austrian for "Tüte", bag), "Rahm" (Austrian/Swiss for "Sahne", cream), "Erdapfel" (Austrian for "Kartoffel", potato), "Velo" (Swiss for "Fahrrad", bicycle), "Grüezi" (Swiss greeting equivalent to "Hallo").
c1-regionalismen.fact: This course teaches standard German (Hochdeutsch) as spoken in Germany as its production target — these regional variants are presented for RECOGNITION only, since a C1 speaker should never be confused encountering them in an Austrian newspaper or a Swiss menu, even without using them personally.

dialogue.native: Im Jänner fahre ich mit dem Velo zur Arbeit, wenn es nicht zu kalt ist.
dialogue.en: In January, I ride my bike to work, if it's not too cold. (Austrian/Swiss vocabulary)

c1-journalistischer-stil.title: Journalistic Register
c1-journalistischer-stil.pattern: compressed headlines, Konjunktiv I attribution, nominal density, neutral tone
c1-journalistischer-stil.explanation: Journalistic German favors compressed headlines (often dropping articles and verbs), heavy use of Konjunktiv I for attributed claims, dense Nominalstil, and a deliberately neutral, distancing tone even when reporting controversial events. Recognizing these conventions is essential for reading news fluently: a headline like "Regierung plant Reform" drops the article "die" that a full sentence would require.
c1-journalistischer-stil.fact: Journalistic texts often layer several C1 features at once — a headline in telegraphic style, followed by a lead paragraph in dense Nominalstil, followed by body text switching to Konjunktiv I the moment a source is quoted — training your eye to notice these shifts makes news texts far more transparent.

dialogue.native: Laut Sprecher solle die Reform bereits im Herbst in Kraft treten.
dialogue.en: According to the spokesperson, the reform is supposed to take effect as early as fall.

c1-literarischer-stil.title: Literary Register
c1-literarischer-stil.pattern: evocative imagery, varied sentence rhythm, sensory detail, complex embedded subordination
c1-literarischer-stil.explanation: Literary German favors evocative imagery, sensory description, and varied sentence rhythm — short sentences for impact alongside long, richly subordinated ones for atmosphere. Compared to journalistic or academic register, it draws more on metaphor, personification, and deliberately unusual word order for effect: "Der Regen tanzte auf dem Dach" (The rain danced on the roof — personification) or fronting an unexpected element for emphasis.
c1-literarischer-stil.fact: Literary texts often deliberately break the "normal" rules the rest of this course has taught — unusual word order, sentence fragments, invented compound words — precisely because breaking a well-understood rule is what creates a stylistic effect. Recognizing this is part of reading literature maturely: not every deviation is an error to flag.

dialogue.native: Der Regen tanzte auf dem Dach, während die Stadt langsam einschlief.

c1-wortstellung-nuancen.title: Advanced Word Order: Emphasis and Extraposition
c1-wortstellung-nuancen.pattern: Vorfeld variation for emphasis; es as a placeholder/dummy subject
c1-wortstellung-nuancen.explanation: German's flexible "Vorfeld" (the single slot before the verb in a main clause) lets a speaker choose what to emphasize by fronting it — not just the subject: "Diesen Film habe ich schon gesehen" (THIS movie I've already seen, emphasizing the object) vs. the neutral "Ich habe diesen Film schon gesehen." The dummy "es" can also fill the Vorfeld when nothing else is fronted, purely to satisfy verb-second word order: "Es regnet" or "Es waren einmal drei Freunde" (Once there were three friends).
c1-wortstellung-nuancen.fact: Fronting for emphasis is a genuine C1 stylistic tool, not just a grammar curiosity: choosing to front the object, a time expression, or even a whole subordinate clause changes what the sentence foregrounds as its topic, without changing the literal propositional content at all — mastering this is part of sounding rhetorically deliberate rather than just grammatically correct.

dialogue.native: Diese Entscheidung hätte ich nicht erwartet.

dialogue.native: Mich hat sie ehrlich gesagt auch überrascht.

c1-nominalisierung-meisterschaft.title: Nominalization Mastery
c1-nominalisierung-meisterschaft.pattern: chaining multiple nominalizations and genitive/prepositional phrases into a single dense sentence
c1-nominalisierung-meisterschaft.explanation: At C1, nominalization moves beyond single conversions into chaining several together within one sentence — a hallmark of academic and highly formal writing: "Die Verzögerung der Fertigstellung des Projekts aufgrund unzureichender Kommunikation zwischen den Abteilungen führte zur Verschiebung der Präsentation." Untangling such sentences means identifying each nominalized "chunk" (Verzögerung, Fertigstellung, Kommunikation, Verschiebung, Präsentation) and how they connect via genitive chains and prepositions.
c1-nominalisierung-meisterschaft.fact: Producing sentences this dense is rarely necessary even at C1 — the real skill being tested is READING them fluently. When you find yourself untangling one, work from the main verb outward, treating each nominalized noun as if it were still hiding its original verb or adjective, one layer at a time.

c1-abtoenung.title: Hedging Language and Subtle Nuance
c1-abtoenung.pattern: sozusagen, gewissermaßen, quasi, im Grunde genommen, gleichsam — softening precision claims
c1-abtoenung.explanation: C1 speakers use hedging language to soften an assertion, signal approximation, or acknowledge nuance without undermining the whole statement: "sozusagen" (so to speak), "gewissermaßen" (in a certain sense), "quasi" (essentially/virtually), "im Grunde genommen" (basically, at bottom), "gleichsam" (as it were, more literary). These let a speaker make a claim while flagging "this isn't perfectly precise, but close enough."
c1-abtoenung.fact: Overusing hedging language sounds evasive, while never using it sounds blunt or overconfident — native speakers calibrate its frequency to context: more hedging in tentative academic claims or diplomatic disagreement, less in direct factual statements. Listening for how often native speakers hedge is a good gauge for your own use.

dialogue.native: Das Projekt ist quasi schon abgeschlossen.

dialogue.native: Im Grunde genommen ja, es fehlen nur noch ein paar Kleinigkeiten.

c1-textsorten.title: Text-Type Awareness: Essay, Speech, Report
c1-textsorten.pattern: matching structure and rhetoric to text type: argumentative essay, persuasive speech, objective report
c1-textsorten.explanation: Different text types demand different structures and rhetorical devices even when covering the same topic. An argumentative essay builds a thesis with evidence and counterarguments; a persuasive speech uses rhetorical questions, repetition (Anapher), and direct address to move an audience; an objective report stays neutral, cites sources, and avoids personal opinion entirely. Recognizing which type you're reading — or need to write — shapes every other choice.
c1-textsorten.fact: A rhetorical question ("Wollen wir wirklich, dass das so weitergeht?") is a persuasive-speech device that would be out of place in an objective report — noticing genre-inappropriate rhetorical devices is itself a sign of critical, C1-level reading, useful both for writing appropriately and for spotting manipulation in texts pretending to be neutral.
